newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FEATURE - Malaysian cat city boasts unique feline museum.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Malaysian cat city boasts unique feline museum.

text.p: Malaysians call it mayau, mao, ngau or miew.
Whatever its name, the cat has always held a special place in many households.
In Kuching, capital of Malaysia's eastern state of Sarawak -- and itself the Malay word for cat -- they even have a museum to call their own.
Jigsaw puzzles featuring cats, wall tiles, books, stamps, decorative plates and other cat-related paraphernalia are on display in the museum on the outskirts of the city.
There are special sections on black cats, cats at play and the role of cats in Japanese and Egyptian culture in the air-conditioned museum, which does not charge an entrance fee.

Colourful posters of movies like "Cat People" and "Cat From Outer Space" are placed near pictures of famous personalities who loved cats, like author Mark Twain and British nursing pioneer Florence Nightingale.
Song albums by the top Malaysian group Alleycats are displayed alongside one by Cat Stevens.
Formerly part of the Sarawak Museum, the exhibits were transferred in 1993 to the present site on the ground floor of the Kuching North City Hall.
HOW CITY WAS NAMED REMAINS A MYSTERY
The special interest for cats in Kuching, a fast-growing city on Borneo island, is hardly surprising given its name.
But the history of how the city -- located along the swift-flowing Sarawak River -- was so named has been long forgotten.
According to local speculation, cats may have been abundant at busy ports along the Sarawak River in the past century.
Sarawak was ruled for more than a century by the so-called White Rajahs from Britain, the Brookes.
"In 1839, James Brooke (the first white Rajah) referred to the town as Kuchin', which might suggest the old word Cochin or port, as in India or Indo-China," the museum display says.

Another theory is the town derived its name in the late 19th Century from a river passing through it. The river was called Sungai Kuching as it passed near a hill covered with fruit trees known locally as Matta Kuching, literally cat's eyes (Nephelium Malaiense).
"Thus, it's settled that in 1876 the town became officially known as Kuching," the museum display says.
KUCHING CATS APPEAR IN VARIOUS FORMS
Today, the cat is as easily identified with eastern Malaysia as two other animal dwellers of the sparsely-populated rainforest state, the hornbill and the orang-utan.
The cat appears in a variety of colours and forms in Kuching -- as city statues, on hotel brochures and as trinkets in tourist shops.
The city's cat connection is a good selling point, said cat-lover Susie Wong, 33. "Singapore's got the lion city. I think it's unique that Kuching has the cat."

Sarawak's 25 indigenous races call it by many names, most with a strong hint of the sound the cat makes. Sarawak's majority race of Ibans calls the cat mayau. The Chinese call the feline mao, the Melanau call it ngau, and the Kenyah, miew.
The museum said Sarawak's "most sought after" breed is nyeng, the tabby, which is found in longhouses across the rainforest interior of the state and in villages.
"There are a lot of cat lovers in Kuching...but it's probably a coincidence," said Jacqueline Kueh, 24, who says she too is fond of the animals.
